clue.text: Attractive European not quite on top of the world

definitions.text: not quite on top of the world

blocks.note: a magnet attracts, so attractive can be magnetic
a Pole is a native of Poland

explanation.surface: A charming continental who is not quite feeling on top of the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite on top of the world' reads like mild gloom, but it is the definition: the magnetic pole lies some distance from the true geographic pole.
explanation.definitionFit: The point a compass needle seeks wanders near, but not exactly at, the planet's northern axis point.

clue.text: A doctor among stubborn types near Swansea

definitions.note: a place description; the answer is a place near Swansea

indicators.note: being among others means sitting inside their group, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification
mules are proverbially stubborn animals

explanation.surface: A doctor practising among obstinate people in a town on the Welsh coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mumbles is a headland and village on Swansea Bay in south Wales, so the definition is a location rather than a description.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mumbles is a seaside headland district just west of the Welsh city, on its bay.

clue.text: At the end of the month, nothing but enthusiasm

indicators.note: only the closing part of the month's name is wanted, so its opening letters are dropped

blocks.note: the eighth month of the year
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A grumble that at the month's end there is nothing left but keenness.
explanation.walkthrough: The last four letters of AUGUST are its end, then O is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Gusto is hearty relish or zest, a synonym for keen eagerness in doing something.

clue.text: First product of sweated labour ?

blocks.note: surface reading: the first goods made in an exploitative sweatshop
setter's reading: labour that makes a person literally sweat, whose first output is the moisture oozing from the skin

explanation.surface: The first goods turned out by a sweatshop's underpaid workers.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweated labour is a phrase for exploited workers; read literally, hard work makes you sweat, and sweat oozing out is the first thing produced.
explanation.definitionFit: Exudation is the oozing of fluid through pores, and perspiration is the classic example of it.

clue.text: One in the eye for horticulturists?

definitions.text: One in the eye for horticulturists

blocks.note: surface reading: a setback or snub, as in a one-in-the-eye moment; also the coloured ring inside the eye
setter's reading: to gardeners the same word names a flowering plant

explanation.surface: A snub aimed at gardeners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One in the eye' is an idiom for a rebuff, but here it is literal: the part of the eye that gardeners also know as a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The coloured ring of the eye shares its name with a popular flowering plant grown by gardeners.

clue.text: A pierrot doing a turn in Africa

definitions.note: a place description; the answer is a city in Africa

indicators.note: a performer doing a turn suggests letters turned about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A white-faced clown performing his act somewhere in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: A pierrot is a French pantomime clown, and a turn is a stage act, which is why the anagram signal hides so well.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretoria is the administrative capital city of South Africa, so it is located on that continent.

clue.text: Without inclination either way

blocks.note: surface reading: having no preference; also having no slope at all
setter's reading: the word reads the same in both directions

explanation.surface: Someone who has no preference for one side or the other.
explanation.walkthrough: Inclination means both a preference and a slope; 'either way' also hints that the word is a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: Something level is flat and horizontal, with no slope towards one side or the other.

clue.text: Alias Walton-on-Thames?

blocks.note: surface reading: the town of that name in Surrey
setter's reading: Izaak Walton fishing on the river, under the name he used for his angler

explanation.surface: Another name for a Surrey town beside the Thames.
explanation.walkthrough: Izaak Walton wrote The Compleat Angler, whose fisherman is called Piscator; Walton-on-Thames is a Surrey town, recast as Walton by the river with a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Piscator is Latin for fisherman and the name of the angler in Walton's book, so it serves as his alias.

clue.text: Tom's eye

blocks.note: surface reading: the eye of someone called Tom, or of a tomcat
setter's reading: Peeping Tom, the voyeur, and slang for an eye

explanation.surface: The eye of a man named Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: Peeping Tom is the legendary Coventry tailor who spied on Lady Godiva; the answer is both a slang eye and a Peeping Tom himself.
explanation.definitionFit: Peepers is slang for eyes, and the word also names the voyeur who spies on others.

clue.text: Unladylike assortment of calumnies

indicators.note: an assortment is a mixed collection, so the letters come out mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lady swapping a string of slanders, which is hardly ladylike behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: Masculine describes qualities associated with men, the opposite of feminine and therefore not befitting a lady.

clue.text: An utter failure, losing it?

blocks.note: surface reading: a complete failure, a total flop
setter's reading: losing the faculty of speech makes someone fail to utter, to speak

explanation.surface: Someone who is a complete flop and losing their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: Utter seems to mean complete but is the verb to speak: when you lose your voice, you fail to utter.
explanation.definitionFit: The voice is the faculty of speaking; lose it and you cannot produce a sound.

clue.text: Half crazy about a couple of ducks in the bath

definitions.note: a place description; the answer is a sponge used in the bath

indicators.note: crazy suggests something disordered, so the letters before it are scrambled
about means around, so the scrambled letters wrap around the birds

blocks.note: taken as written
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, written O; two of them

explanation.surface: Someone half mad about a pair of rubber ducks in the tub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half crazy' looks like one idea, but the word half is the anagram material; OO sits inside its rearrangement LFAH.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofah is the dried fibrous gourd used as a scrubbing sponge when washing in a tub.

clue.text: Paper surely not for the head of the class?

blocks.note: surface reading: a size of writing paper

blocks.clueFragment: surely not for the head of the class
blocks.note: setter's reading: split in two, the name is the dunce's hat worn by the worst pupil, never the top one

explanation.surface: A sheet of paper that is surely not meant for the top pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: The paper size takes its name from an old fool's-cap watermark; split it and you have the dunce's cap, worn at the bottom of the class.
explanation.definitionFit: Foolscap is a traditional large size of writing and printing sheet, once common for legal documents.

clue.text: The height of achievement

blocks.note: surface reading: the greatest possible success
setter's reading: the literal highest point, reached by a climber

explanation.surface: The greatest success anyone could hope for.
explanation.definitionFit: A summit is the highest point of a mountain, and figuratively the peak of someone's success.

clue.text: They're not lost among elephants

blocks.note: surface reading: some things that never go missing in a herd
setter's reading: the saying that an elephant never forgets

explanation.surface: Things that never go astray in a herd of elephants.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'an elephant never forgets' is the key.
explanation.definitionFit: Memories are recollections of the past, which the proverb says elephants always keep and never lose.

clue.text: Kipling's impostor

blocks.note: surface reading: a fraud or swindler in a Kipling story
setter's reading: in his poem If, Kipling pairs Triumph with one of 'those two impostors'

explanation.surface: A fraud from one of Kipling's tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's If tells us to meet with Triumph and Disaster and treat those two impostors just the same.
explanation.definitionFit: In the poem If, catastrophe is one of two impostors to be treated with equal calm.

clue.text: Two are heard in a haunted house

definitions.text: Two are heard in a haunted house

blocks.clueFragment: Two are heard in a haunted house
blocks.note: surface reading: a couple of ghosts or noises heard in a spooky building
setter's reading: each of the two words opens with a breathed h sound, which phoneticians name for the breath

explanation.surface: A couple of spectral sounds audible in a spooky mansion.
explanation.walkthrough: The words haunted and house each start with a sounded h, the breathy consonant that grammarians call by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: An aspirate is a breathed h sound in phonetics, and both of those words begin with one.

clue.text: Back in this sporting role

blocks.note: surface reading: returning to a sporting position
setter's reading: a back is a player whose job is to protect the goal

explanation.surface: A player returning to a familiar position in the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in' reads as returning, but a back is the position itself in football or hockey.
explanation.definitionFit: In team sports a back is a rearward player whose job is to stop opponents scoring.

clue.text: No reason to be so (if out of sight?)

blocks.note: surface reading: there is no cause to feel that way; also being with no reason, out of one's mind
setter's reading: out of sight, out of mind, the proverb

explanation.surface: There is no cause to feel that way just because someone has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of sight, out of mind' supplies the joke: losing one's reason is being out of one's mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone demented has lost their reason entirely and is, in the old phrase, out of their mind.

clue.text: Help a ship's hands give, say, for a time

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the phrase and listen for a single word

blocks.note: help given by deckhands, the crew who work on deck

explanation.surface: Volunteers helping the sailors for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: Ship's hands work on deck, so the help they give is deck aid, which said quickly is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A decade is a period of ten years, so it is a span of time.

clue.text: Lindbergh's St Louis-style gumption

blocks.note: first meaning: Lindbergh's plane was the ... of St Louis
second meaning: courage and pluck

explanation.surface: Charles Lindbergh showing pluck in true St Louis fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Lindbergh flew the Atlantic solo in 1927 in the Spirit of St Louis.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirit is the first word of the plane's name and also means courage or mettle, much like gumption.

clue.text: Exchanges include one of these abusive speeches

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: trading is exchanging goods
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Heated arguments that include one bout of angry ranting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exchanges' suggests arguments, but here it means trades. The I goes inside TRADES after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long angry speech of criticism or denunciation, so abusive speeches fit in the plural.

clue.text: The craft of many pronaos prognosticators

definitions.note: craft is plural here, as the answer is

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many
oracles foretold the future from temples; a pronaos is the porch of a Greek temple

explanation.surface: The skill shared by many prophets who sat in temple porches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The craft' looks like a skill or trade, but it means small boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Coracles are small round wicker boats covered in hide, and boats are craft.

clue.text: 25 getting French priest round the bend

indicators.note: round means encircling, so the cleric's title goes around the number

blocks.note: curé is a French parish priest
the answer to 25 is five, the Roman numeral V

explanation.surface: Someone being driven crazy by a French priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round the bend' is slang for mad, but here round is the container signal and the bend is the definition. V goes inside CURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A curve is a bend, as in a road that bends or curves away.

clue.text: He should certainly mind his own business

definitions.text: He should certainly mind his own business

blocks.note: surface reading: a busybody being told not to meddle
setter's reading: literally look after the shop he runs

explanation.surface: A nosy man being told to keep out of other people's affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A trader runs a commercial concern of his own, so tending it is exactly his job.

clue.text: No busy bee, clubman Wooster

blocks.note: first meaning: a male bee that does no work in the hive
second meaning: Bertie Wooster is a member of the ... Club in P. G. Wodehouse's stories

explanation.walkthrough: Bertie Wooster, P. G. Wodehouse's idle young gentleman, belongs to the Drones Club in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The idle male honeybee and a member of Wodehouse's fictional gentlemen's club share the same name.

clue.text: So many giving the victory sign

definitions.text: So many giving the victory sign

blocks.clueFragment: So many giving the victory sign
blocks.note: surface reading: a crowd all holding up two fingers in triumph
setter's reading: the sign is the letter V, which is also a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A large crowd all raising two fingers in celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: Churchill's V for victory sign is the letter V, the Roman numeral for this number.
explanation.definitionFit: Five is written V in Roman numerals, the same letter as the victory salute.

clue.text: “ In a —— -nighted December ” (Keats)

blocks.note: surface reading: an opening line from a lyric with a word missing
setter's reading: the line opens a short Keats poem about winter and its gloomy nights

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word completes the first line of a short Keats poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic form of dreary, describing December nights that are long, dark and gloomy.

clue.text: Not suitable timber to build a stable?

definitions.text: Not suitable timber to build a stable

blocks.note: surface reading: constructing a building for horses
setter's reading: stable as an adjective, firm and steady, which floating wood is not

explanation.surface: Wood that would not do for putting up a horse's shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: Stable looks like a noun for a horse's home, but the joke is the adjective: wood that drifts is anything but steady.
explanation.definitionFit: Driftwood is timber washed up by or floating on the sea, wandering wherever the current takes it.

clue.text: Unangelic characteristic of impetuous fools

blocks.note: surface reading: some wicked trait, unlike an angel
setter's reading: fools rush in where angels fear to tread, from Pope

explanation.surface: A devilish trait shown by reckless idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope's line 'fools rush in where angels fear to tread': angels fear, fools do not.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearlessness is the absence of dread, the quality that lets rash people rush in where cautious ones hold back.
